strengths: Clear motivation and framing: the interleaving of reasoning-guided search and search-informed reasoning in multi-hop claim verification is well articulated, and Figure 1's motivating example (implicit bridging facts) concretely illustrates why static decomposition or single-pass retrieval is insufficient.

The coordinated two-agent design is trained end-to-end with GRPO using only outcome-based rewards (plus a lightweight LLM-judge reward for the search agent), avoiding intermediate supervision; the alternating 'coordinated agent training' schedule with data synthesis from reasoning rollouts is a reasonable and clearly described mechanism (Algorithm 1).

Ablations are targeted and informative: single-agent vs. multi-agent comparison (Table 2) partially controls for the RL-training confound, the coordination-rounds experiment (Table 3), and the F1 vs. LLM-as-a-Judge reward analysis (Figures 4-5) provide behavioral insight rather than only aggregate numbers.

Evaluation spans three benchmarks (HOVER, EX-FEVER, CHECKWHY), including an out-of-distribution test on CHECKWHY, and results are consistent across hop depths, with the largest gains in the harder 3-hop/4-hop settings.
Reproducibility is comparatively good for this line of work: prompts, DSPy signatures, synthesized training data examples, hardware, and hyperparameters are provided in the appendices.
weaknesses: Baseline fairness is a core concern: HARIS is an RL-trained, in-domain-trained system (7,200 training examples from EX-FEVER/HOVER), while most baselines are zero/few-shot GPT-4o pipelines. The single-agent ablation helps, but there is no comparison against equally RL-trained search-LLM baselines adapted to claim verification (e.g., Search-R1, R1-Searcher), so the source of the improvement (hierarchical design vs. task-specific RL training vs. more search calls) is not fully isolated.

Statistical rigor is limited: evaluation uses only 500 sampled instances per setting, no significance tests, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed/variance reporting, despite gaps over strong baselines being modest (~2-3 points in many settings).

The LLM-as-a-Judge reward is coarse (binary yes/no via GPT-4o-mini over pseudo ground-truth answers also generated by GPT-4o), creating circularity and reward-hacking risk; no analysis of judge reliability or reward-hacking behavior is provided.

The CHECKWHY generalization claim is weak: only positive samples are used, reducing it to a retrieval-support task rather than full verification, and this caveat deserves more prominence than a footnote.

Some claims are overstated or inconsistent with the evidence: 'greatly advancing multi-hop claim verification' overstates 2-3 point gains; Table 3 actually shows N=1 better on HOVER 4-hop F1, contradicting the text that more coordination rounds 'generally improve' performance; Appendix sections B.1/B.2 are duplicated text.

Novelty is incremental: the component techniques (tag-based rollout control, GRPO, loss masking, reward shaping) closely follow Search-R1/R1-Searcher-style work; the main novel element is the alternating hierarchical co-training, which is sensible but a relatively small architectural delta.
No code or artifact release is mentioned, which limits practical reproducibility despite the detailed appendix.
Only a 4B model is studied and training details are given, but scaling behavior (acknowledged in Limitations) is unexplored, leaving the generality of the coordinated-training benefit unclear.

strengths: The core research question—coordinating reasoning-driven search and search-informed reasoning for multi-hop claim verification—is well motivated and clearly relevant to computational linguistics, and the paper articulates the interleaved nature of the problem better than many prior decomposition-based works.

The coordinated two-agent training procedure (alternating GRPO between a high-level reasoning agent and a low-level search agent with synthesized QA data) is described at a level of detail that is mostly reconstructable, with hyperparameters, hardware, retrieval setup, and prompt templates provided in the appendix.

The paper includes several targeted ablations (single-agent vs. multi-agent, coordination rounds N, F1 vs. LLM-as-a-Judge rewards) that go beyond a single main results table, and the case studies (Figures 6–9) provide concrete behavioral evidence supporting the design choice.
The main results show consistent gains over prompted baselines across HOVER, EX-FEVER, and CHECKWHY, including in the harder 3-hop and 4-hop settings.
weaknesses: The baseline comparison is not fair in its current form. All prompted baselines use GPT-4o (Search-o1 uses QwQ-32B), while HARIS is a Qwen3-4B model additionally RL fine-tuned on 7,200 in-domain examples drawn from the training sets of the very benchmarks used for evaluation. The gains therefore conflate fine-tuning, in-domain training data, model choice, and the proposed architecture. A GPT-4o-based or fine-tuned-GPT-4o variant of the same pipeline, or an RL-trained single agent of the same size compared under identical budgets, is needed to isolate the contribution; the single-agent ablation partially addresses this but is only reported against HARIS, not against the external baselines.

The generalization claim on CHECKWHY is weak: evaluation is restricted to 500 positive-only samples (binary accuracy on a single class), which is a much easier setting than the original benchmark and weakens the interpretation that HARIS 'handles causally structured claims'.

Reported improvements over the strongest baseline (Search-o1) are modest (e.g., 69.40 vs. 69.00 on HOVER 2-hop), and no statistical significance testing, variance across seeds, or multiple runs are reported; single-run results on 500 sampled instances make several comparisons difficult to distinguish from noise.

The search-agent reward depends on a GPT-4o-generated pseudo ground truth and a GPT-4o-mini judge with a binary yes/no signal; this introduces an unquantified noise/hacking source, couples results to closed commercial APIs, and hampers reproducibility. No code, data, or trained checkpoints are stated as released.

Novelty is incremental. Two-level reasoning/search decomposition plus GRPO-based RL training with tag-based rollouts and retrieved-token masking closely follows established recipes (Search-R1, R1-Searcher, DeepRAG, ReMA, QACheck-style iterative QA). The main novelty is applying and alternating this recipe for claim verification, which is useful but not a substantial methodological advance.

Supporting evidence for interpretability and the 'reduced retrieval noise' claims is anecdotal (case studies and one figure of search-call counts); no quantitative analysis of verification-chain quality, evidence precision/recall, or question quality is provided.

Several details undermine rigor and polish: Table 3 shows N=3 actually degrades 4-hop HOVER performance while the text claims improvement 'generally'; appendix sections B.1 and B.2 are duplicated verbatim; and the writing contains multiple grammatical errors ('an joint process', 'This process synthesize', 'colloraborate'), suggesting insufficient proofreading.

The scope is limited to binary labels (Support/Refute), and the limitations section acknowledges this, but many fact-verification benchmarks require a NotEnoughInfo class; claims of 'greatly advancing multi-hop claim verification' should be tempered accordingly.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper explicitly targets the reciprocal interplay between reasoning-guided search and search-informed reasoning in multi-hop claim verification, and the two-agent design (high-level reasoning agent issuing questions; low-level search agent iteratively retrieving) is a natural and interpretable instantiation of this idea.

Technically complete training recipe: coordinated two-stage alternating GRPO training with outcome-based rewards for the reasoning agent and LLM-as-a-Judge rewards for the search agent, retrieved-token loss masking, and a data synthesis procedure that aligns search-agent training questions with the reasoning agent's distribution (Algorithm 1, Appendix A.4).

Strong empirical results: consistent gains over GPT-4o-based baselines and Search-o1 on HOVER (2/3/4-hop) and EX-FEVER (2/3-hop), with the largest margins in the harder 3-hop and 4-hop settings, plus generalization to CHECKWHY.

Meaningful ablations: (i) an RL-trained single-agent baseline shows the bi-level decomposition itself (not just RL training) contributes to the gains; (ii) coordination rounds N are varied; (iii) the reward-design comparison (F1 vs LLM-as-a-Judge) provides an interesting behavioral analysis linking reward style to search-call frequency and downstream verification reward.

Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, hardware, retrieval setup (corpus, embedder, top-k), prompt templates, DSPy signatures for rewards and data synthesis, and qualitative case studies in the appendix.
Relevant to ACL scope: claim verification is a core NLP task, and the framework speaks to active areas (agentic RAG, RL for LLM search, fact-checking interpretability).
weaknesses: Baseline comparability is imperfect: most baselines use GPT-4o in a prompted (non-RL) setting while HARIS is RL-trained on a Qwen3-4B using the training splits of the same evaluation benchmarks. Although the RL-trained single-agent ablation partially mitigates this, the comparison conflates the hierarchical design with RL training and in-domain tuning; prompting-only baselines are at a disadvantage, and there is no RL-trained prompt-engineering baseline of matched compute.

Evaluation rigor is limited: only 500 stratified samples per setting, no variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance testing; several margins over the strongest baseline (Search-o1) are small (e.g., HOVER 2-hop: 69.40 vs 69.00 accuracy), so claimed superiority on those settings is not firmly established.

Ablation results are mixed but reported optimistically: Table 3 shows HOVER 4-hop actually degrades from N=1 (60.87 F1) to N=3 (59.84 F1), yet Section 5.2 states that increasing N 'generally improves overall performance' without acknowledging the inconsistency.

The search-agent reward pipeline introduces unvalidated noise: pseudo ground-truth answers are generated by GPT-4o and judged by GPT-4o-mini, with no human validation of either the synthesized answers or the judge's reliability; reward-hacking risk (verbose outputs judged 'useful') is not analyzed beyond a coarse call-frequency comparison.

Retrieval conditions are not uniform across methods: HARIS and most baselines use E5-small/top-3 over the FlashRAG Wikipedia corpus, but FOLK is grounded via the Google Search API, making that comparison questionable; the paper does not discuss this discrepancy.

Only positive CHECKWHY samples are evaluated (accuracy-only), which weakens the generalization claim; the binary Support/Refute scope excludes 'Neutral'/'NotEnoughInfo' labels common in fact verification (acknowledged in Limitations, but it limits external validity).

Writing and presentation issues: duplicated and identical Appendix sections B.1 and B.2, typos ('an joint process', 'colloraborate'), a placeholder-style Figure 4/5, and a missing reason for selecting N=3 over other configurations.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior agentic RAG and multi-agent RL work (Search-R1, R1-Searcher, Search-o1, ReMA, LoCal); the hierarchical reasoner/searcher decomposition applied to claim verification is a reasonable contribution but builds closely on established components.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem (multi-hop claim verification requiring interleaved reasoning and retrieval), and the hierarchical two-agent decomposition (high-level reasoning agent + low-level search agent) is clearly motivated by the reciprocal relationship between reasoning and search.

The training methodology is reasonably well described: GRPO with outcome-based rewards for the reasoning agent, LLM-as-a-Judge rewards for the search agent, coordinated alternating training (Algorithm 1), and retrieved-token loss masking, with hyperparameters and hardware reported in the appendix.

Empirical coverage is comparatively broad: main results on EX-FEVER and HOVER across hop counts, out-of-distribution evaluation on CHECKWHY, direct same-backbone comparisons (Qwen3-4B, Table 5), single-agent vs. multi-agent ablation (Table 2), SFT comparison (Table 6), model-scaling ReAct comparison (Table 7), coordination-rounds ablation (Table 3), and a reward-design ablation (F1 vs. LLM-as-a-Judge, Table 4, Figures 4-5).
The reliability of the LLM-as-a-Judge reward is validated with a human evaluation (Cohen's Kappa 0.81, 93.3% agreement), with annotation details and payment/consent disclosed.

Prompt templates, DSPy signatures, synthesized training data examples, and qualitative rollout case studies (Figures 6-9) are provided, supporting interpretability claims and aiding reproducibility of the setup.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: RL-trained search-augmented LLMs (Search-R1, R1-Searcher, DeepRAG, Search-o1) and multi-agent fact-checking pipelines (LoCal, BiDeV) are well established; the core contribution is essentially a hierarchical two-agent instantiation with alternating GRPO training, and the paper does not deeply analyze what specifically the decoupling buys beyond the single-agent RL baseline (e.g., why the gains emerge, or failure modes of the hierarchical design).

Evaluation has methodological caveats: CHECKWHY evaluation uses only positive samples, so the reported accuracy is trivially inflated by a biased 'Support' predictor, weakening the generalization claim; evaluation uses only 500 sampled instances per setting with no variance, seeds, or significance testing.

There are apparent errors undermining confidence in the reported numbers: in Table 5, the FOLK row's EX-FEVER results (80.12/80.20, 73.93/74.20) are identical to the HARIS row, suggesting a copy/paste mistake in a table meant to substantiate the paper's central comparative claim; footnote 1 ('Code:') is empty, so no code or data release is available.

Comparison fairness is partially confounded: main-table baselines use GPT-4o (and Search-o1 uses a 32B model) while HARIS uses an RL-trained Qwen3-4B; although Table 5 attempts a same-backbone comparison, the suspected error in that table prevents a clean apples-to-apples validation.

The search agent's training reward depends on pseudo ground-truth answers generated by GPT-4o, introducing a potential propagation of judge bias into training; the ~10% filtering is described only briefly, and the sensitivity of results to this synthesis quality is not analyzed.

The scope is limited to binary verification on Wikipedia-based benchmarks with a small (4B) backbone; the limitations section acknowledges this, but there is no analysis of how the framework handles 'NEI'/multi-label settings, ambiguous claims, or non-Wikipedia retrieval corpora.

Writing quality is uneven: duplicated appendix text (C.2/C.3 repeat identical content), some overclaiming in phrasing ('greatly advancing multi-hop claim verification'), and the connection between the motivating Figure 1 scenario and the experimental evidence is asserted rather than measured (e.g., no quantitative analysis of bridging-fact discovery).

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem (multi-hop claim verification requiring interleaved reasoning and retrieval), and the proposed hierarchical decomposition into a reasoning agent and a search agent is clearly motivated and easy to follow.

The coordinated/alternating GRPO training scheme (Algorithm 1) is well specified, including reward design, retrieved-token loss masking, and training data synthesis, which supports reproducibility of the core method.

The experimental section is relatively broad: results on EX-FEVER, HOVER, and CHECKWHY, plus ablations covering single-agent vs. multi-agent, coordination rounds N, LLM-as-a-Judge vs. F1 rewards, SFT comparison, ReAct scaling across 4B/8B/14B, and a direct same-base-model comparison (Table 5).

A human evaluation of the LLM-as-a-Judge reward (Cohen's Kappa 0.81, 93.3% agreement) is a good practice, and qualitative case studies (Figures 6-9) illustrate the behavioral differences between single- and multi-agent rollouts.
The paper includes an honest limitations section (4B model only, binary verification only).
weaknesses: Table 5 contains an apparent copy-paste error: the FOLK row reports EX-FEVER numbers identical to HARIS (80.12/80.20 and 73.93/74.20), which undermines confidence in the reported results; the Search-o1 row referenced in footnote 11 is also missing from the table.

The main comparison (Table 1) is confounded: HARIS is a fine-tuned Qwen3-4B while most baselines use GPT-4o and Search-o1 uses QwQ-32B. The same-model comparison in Table 5 mitigates this but is marred by the errors above, and Table 1 conflates model quality with method quality.

The CHECKWHY evaluation uses only positive samples and reports accuracy, which is not a meaningful metric under this protocol (predicting 'Support' always yields perfect accuracy) and weakens the generalization claim.

Contradictions between results and claims: Table 3 shows N=1 outperforming N=3 on HOVER-4hop (60.87/61.80 vs. 59.84/61.00), yet the text states increasing N 'generally leads to stronger performance' and the main results use N=3; no explanation is given.

Gains over the strongest baselines are small on several settings (e.g., HOVER-2hop: 69.40 vs. 69.00 for Search-o1), and no statistical significance testing, variance across seeds, or confidence intervals are reported anywhere.

Novelty is modest: the approach largely combines existing components (tag-based agentic search rollouts from Search-R1/R1-Searcher-style methods, GRPO, and a reasoner/searcher decomposition). The claim of being 'among the first RL-based cooperative agent approach for claim verification' is overclaimed given closely related multi-agent RL work.

The search agent reward relies on GPT-4o-mini judging against pseudo ground-truth answers generated by GPT-4o, creating potential circularity and reward noise; the human validation, while positive, covers only 150 held-out samples.

Reproducibility concerns: the code link in the paper is empty, and there are presentation defects (duplicated Section C.2/C.3 text, unexplained footnote placement) suggesting the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

The rationale for the two-agent design is asserted rather than analyzed: the claimed specialization/traceability benefits are supported only by anecdotes, not by quantitative analysis of agent behaviors or error types.

strengths: The central problem—interleaving reasoning and iterative retrieval for multi-hop claim verification—is well-motivated, and Figure 1 provides a convincing illustration of why static decomposition or single-pass retrieval fails on implicit bridging facts.

The framework is cleanly specified: the high/low-level agent rollouts, tag-based interaction protocol, GRPO-based rewards (Eq. 1-4), and the two-stage Coordinated Agent Training (Algorithm 1) are all described precisely enough to understand and reimplement.

The empirical evaluation is broad and unusually thorough: main comparisons on HOVER, EX-FEVER, and CHECKWHY across 2/3/4-hop settings, plus ablations covering single-agent vs. multi-agent (Table 2), coordination rounds N (Table 3), LLM-as-a-Judge vs. F1 rewards with behavioral analysis (Tables 4, Figures 4-5), SFT comparison (Table 6), and ReAct scaling across 4B/8B/14B backbones (Table 7). These ablations genuinely support the design choices rather than just the headline numbers.

Consistent gains on the harder 3-hop and 4-hop settings, where the proposed decomposition should matter most, strengthens the causal claim that coordination of reasoning and search (rather than generic RL fine-tuning) drives the improvement.
Human evaluation of the LLM-as-a-Judge reward (Cohen's Kappa 0.81, 93.3% agreement, with platform/consent/compensation details) is a responsible treatment of a known weak point of LLM-judged rewards.
Good transparency on hardware, hyperparameters, retrieval setup, prompts (Tables 8-10), and data synthesis with examples (Table 11), and an honest Limitations section.
weaknesses: Table 5 contains a clear error: the FOLK row is identical to the HARIS row (80.12/80.20, 73.93/74.20), which is also implausible since Qwen3-4B-based FOLK would otherwise beat GPT-4o-based FOLK (75.55/75.80) on EX-FEVER. This copy-paste defect, together with the duplicated C.2/C.3 appendix sections and the empty 'Code:' footnote, undermines confidence in the results' curation and weakens reproducibility as submitted.

The main comparison (Table 1) is confounded: baselines run on GPT-4o (Search-o1 on QwQ-32B) while HARIS is a fine-tuned Qwen3-4B. The intended control (Table 5) is the table with the error, so the cleanest apples-to-apples evidence is currently corrupted. The corrected table is essential before conference acceptance.

No statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple-seed results are reported; evaluation uses 500 stratified samples per setting, so differences of ~1-3 F1 points (e.g., HOVER 2-hop 69.31 vs. 69.00 for Search-o1) may not be robust. Significance analysis on the multi-hop settings would substantially strengthen the claims.

The LLM-as-a-Judge reward is coarse and potentially hackable: it is a binary GPT-4o-mini 'yes/no' usefulness judgment against pseudo ground-truth answers generated by GPT-4o. The human validation (150 samples, one panel) is welcome but limited; sensitivity of training to judge model choice or prompt wording is unexamined.

The coordinated alternating training is heuristic: N=1 vs. N=3 is the only round comparison (Table 3, with one metric regressing), and there is no analysis of training stability, reward collapse, or why alternation avoids the known co-adaptation pathologies of joint multi-agent RL.

Novelty is moderate: hierarchical reasoning/search decomposition and GRPO with retrieved-token masking largely recombine existing components (Search-R1, R1-Searcher, DeepRAG, ReMA, Search-o1). The claim of being 'among the first RL-based cooperative agent approach for claim verification' is defensible but the contribution is application-level rather than methodologically new.

CHECKWHY evaluation is restricted to positive samples only, which weakens the generalization claim; binary labels throughout exclude 'Neutral'/'NotEnoughInfo' classes, limiting comparability to the full benchmarks.
